entities.name: Hanno the Elder
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Hanno the Elder was a Carthaginian general who played a significant, albeit ultimately unsuccessful, role in the final stages of the Second Punic War (218–201 BCE). Distinguished from other prominent Carthaginians of the same name, particularly Hanno, son of Bomilcar, this Hanno served as a key subordinate commander under Mago Barca in North Africa. His military career is primarily defined by his engagement against the formidable Roman forces led by Scipio Africanus, marking a critical juncture in Carthage's defense of its homeland.

Hanno's most notable military involvement occurred during the Roman invasion of Africa. He commanded a substantial force of Carthaginian and Numidian troops, forming a crucial part of Mago Barca's army, which aimed to repel Scipio's advance. His strategic movements and engagements culminated in the disastrous Battle of the Great Plains in 203 BCE. In this decisive confrontation, Scipio employed a cunning maneuver, setting fire to the Carthaginian and Numidian camps at night, followed by a direct assault. Hanno, along with Mago, suffered a crushing defeat, with thousands of their soldiers killed or captured, severely weakening Carthage's ability to resist.

The defeat at the Great Plains, in which Hanno was personally captured by Roman forces, had profound consequences for Carthage. It directly paved the way for Scipio Africanus's continued advance and set the stage for the ultimate Roman victory at the Battle of Zama a year later. Hanno's capture demoralized the Carthaginian leadership and populace, signaling the imminent collapse of their resistance and the end of their ambitions for Mediterranean dominance. His fate underscored the military superiority of Rome in the conflict's final phase.
